Our curriculum

Whole-person learning means educating the full range of a young person’s capacities—not only intellect, but also curiosity, creativity, emotional life, relationships, embodied experience, practical skill, and sense of purpose.

Educational values

We practice a form of whole-person education that is both new and inspired by longstanding alternative-educational traditions, aiming to draw out the one-of-a-kind qualities and purposes of each individual, in relationship to others and to the natural world. Each of these areas of human potential is also an educational value unto itself: a core good that expresses what we think education is for, and that guides our learning and teaching in its own way.

Self-Motivation and Engagement
How we follow our curiosity and persevere in what comes of it; how we show up to the learning process and to our efforts more generally.
Self-Understanding and Expression
How we discover who we are, come to know and accept ourselves and share that with the world.
Relational Capacity and Interdependence
How we find mutual support and kinship with others across difference.
Connection to Place
How we cultivate connection with the more-than-human world and belonging in community.
Knowledge Foundations
How we come to know the world, and cultivate skills that will sustain us in it.
Responsibility and Purpose
How we offer something meaningful back to the world that has shaped us, and how we shape it in turn.
Educational Vision (PDF, 13 pages)

Self-directed learning, together

Self-directed learning, together is the name we've given to our learning and teaching model. It is a hybrid approach that is animated by the above values, and that balances student-led learning with teacher-initiated educational experiences, peer learning, and participation in school culture and community life. Students shape their own learning goals, projects, and pathways, while also engaging in interdisciplinary, project-based curriculum designed by teachers and linked to core competencies.

This balancing of student and adult leadership in learning is understood as a productive tension that guides practice rather than a problem to be resolved.

Seven core subject areas

At Canoe Valley School, this approach comes to life through interdisciplinary, project-based work weaving together seven core subject areas:

Communication Arts
Reading, writing, storytelling, rhetoric, deep listening, media production, and foreign languages.
Quantitative and Spatial Reasoning
Arithmetic, geometry, algebra, statistics, modeling, spatial thinking, and systems thinking.
Social Sciences and Community Life
History, philosophy, sociology, geography, economics, psychology, civic engagement, and community stewardship.
Scientific Inquiry and Ecological Arts
Observation, experimentation, biology, ecology, chemistry, physics, geology, botany, horticulture, regenerative agriculture, and land management.
Practical Life and Wellness
Health, nutrition, cooking, repair, hospitality, personal finance, household management, and everyday practical skills.
Fine and Practical Arts
Drawing, painting, printmaking, ceramics, movement, music, folk arts, woodworking, and fiber arts.
Appropriate Design and Technology
Design thinking, architecture, landscape design, sustainable technologies, carpentry, fabrication, and computer science.

“In my 30 years as an educator, I’ve come to understand how important it is for people to have a genuine experience of the place where they live and learn. Place-based education gives students the opportunity not only to learn about the world, but to experience it directly—to explore, to ask questions, to work alongside other people, and to develop a sense of meaning, purpose, and confidence. As a science educator, I encourage healthy skepticism, but I also know that skepticism can become something very different when people are surrounded by fear, misinformation, and apocalyptic thinking. There is real value in stepping outside, paying attention to the natural world, and sharing an experience that is physically real and immediate with other human beings. Those experiences can help us become more grounded in the world rather than more fearful of it. That is one of the things I find so compelling about Canoe Valley School.”

Birgitta, Prospective Teacher

Day to day

Self-Directed, Project-Based Learning

Students learn through interdisciplinary projects that replace traditional classes, and that balance their interests and lived experience with teacher-initiated experiences and project arcs.

Play and Exploration

Students have ample time for purely self-chosen, open-ended activities that are understood as foundational modes of learning, rich sources of future projects, and essential supports for wellbeing.

Reading and Math Foundations Program

Depending on interest, the school may provide a daily independent reading program inspired by the Book Whisperer model, and a regular math practice program inspired by the Math for Love model (think puzzles, games, rich tasks).

Mentorship

Students and teachers engage in regular 1-on-1 and group mentorship sessions that support project design, competency pathways, problem-solving, and emotional wellbeing.

Peer Learning

Students learn in mixed-age communities where collaboration, observation, shared projects, and participation in school culture spark their learning and development.

Learning Goals and Competency Pathways

Projects are linked to a focused and distilled set of core competencies through what we call competency pathways. These are ways of engaging with core skills and knowledge that evolve over time, with increasing student ownership from the lower to the upper level and attention to students’ expected post-secondary paths.

Documenting Learning

Learning is documented through multimedia portfolios and collaboratively written learning narratives that reflect engagement, expression, challenges, and growth over time. There are semesterly collaboration and service-learning requirements, as well as a capstone service-learning project.

Electives

Electives deepen and extend the core learning program. A list of offerings is shaped collaboratively by students and teachers.

School Culture and Community Life

To deepen whole-person learning we envision daily gathering circles, weekly check-in circles, school rituals, teambuilding activities, quarterly showcases, and (especially in the upper level) committee work that supports the life of the school.

Co-Curricular Activities

Co-curricular activities are interwoven with the school’s core curriculum. They include expeditions, apprenticeships, committee work, service-learning, and partnerships with community organizations.

A note on inclusion

The whole-person learning program outlined here provides clear paths to cultivating a welcoming and inclusive school campus, especially in terms of our focus on self-affirmation, expression, and respect for difference. We believe schools thrive when students feel safe being themselves, and when curriculum and teaching is responsive to differences in students’ unique lived experiences, abilities, and ways of seeing the world.

“As a homeschooling parent of children with multiple learning differences—including dyslexia, dysgraphia, dyscalculia, and ADHD—I know how important it is to have an environment that embraces those differences and allows students to learn at their own pace and in ways that build on their strengths. When our children reach high school age, those alternative educational options become much more limited. Canoe Valley School fills this gap. We are excited to see it come to fruition and to have a place where our children can continue learning in an environment that fosters community, confidence, curiosity, and the skills that are meaningful to them.”

Natasha, Parent of Prospective Students
